speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) what other programmes beyond the artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled tools on Singapore Student Learning Space will be put in place to develop baseline AI literacy of students; (b) whether there are plans to launch AI coding programmes in the curriculum; (c) if so, when will such programmes be targeted to be launched; and (d) whether such programmes will be run by teachers or third party service providers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: MOE recognises that AI will become increasingly pervasive in the workplace and in our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To prepare our students and workforce, MOE develops students’ foundational knowledge of AI and promotes its safe and responsible use in schools and at the Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Educators in schools and IHLs are provided with guidance, resources and training to effectively harness it to enhance learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students acquire relevant digital literacies, such as understanding AI, its uses and limitations, and ethical considerations in the course of learning different subjects.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students also have opportunities to further their learning through school-based programmes, such as co-curricular activities, Applied Learning Programmes (ALPs) and enrichment programmes, which may be taught by teachers, industry partners and service providers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One example is the AI Student Outreach Programme conducted by AI Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students from the autonomous universities and the Institute of Technical Education make up the remaining 23% of applicants.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Besides knowledge of AI, schools and IHLs have measures to guard against the risks of AI.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In schools, students are taught cyber wellness skills, which include evaluating information and identifying fake news including those transmitted through AI systems, understanding data security, privacy and responsible online behaviours.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Teachers also guide students to use AI to support their learning, emphasising ethics related to the use of data and AI, such as the importance of integrity and proper data handling.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Teachers at Temasek Primary School taught students to use an AI tool called Stable Diffusion, which is a generative AI image-generator, when learning about sustainability concepts as part of the school's science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) ALP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Guided by their teachers, students learn how to write prompts, evaluate the effectiveness of their prompts and adjust them to improve the quality of the generated images as they create an e-book to advocate sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Another example: students at Montfort Secondary School learn AI through their STEM ALP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students learn the basic AI applications, such as image recognition, chatbots and smart assistants that use natural language processing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students build on this knowledge and further apply it in the Design and Technology subject to design products, such as a blockchain-inspired smart savings application that tracks spending habits and automates money deposits.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yet another example: at Peirce Secondary School, they use generative AI tools in coursework subjects like Design and Technology, and Nutrition and Food Science.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Design and Technology teachers guide their students to use generative AI tools like ChatGPT and Vizcom to generate new ideas for their products, develop their ability to sketch, visualise and imagine solutions for their prototypes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At Yuan Ching Secondary School, students also use AI to generate ideas for their Nutrition and Food Science projects.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In both schools, students are taught to evaluate the credibility of AI-generated content by corroborating it with other reliable information sources.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Students are also taught to acknowledge the use of AI tools and other sources in their reports.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At a higher level, Anderson Serangoon Junior College partnered AI Singapore to introduce students to foundational learning in AI.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Through a jointly organised event, "Prepping for an AI career revolution", students learn about AI and its use cases and engage in a dialogue with industry leaders.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Anderson Serangoon Junior College also developed the infocomms technology (ICT) Champions Programme to enhance digital literacy and skills amongst interested students.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At St Hilda's Primary School, teachers guide students to use customised recommended resources for self-learning or embark on a different lesson if they wish to explore a different sub-topic.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At Rosyth School, before using the ALS, students undergo an introductory module on how AI can be used and its ethical considerations to ensure students use AI safely and holistically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At Temasek Polytechnic's Diploma in Interior Architecture and Design, students are taught to use AI tools to aid them in the design process, such as using ChatGPT to generate design statements and Midjourney to generate reference images.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singapore University of Technology and Design's Design and Artificial Intelligence Programme equips our students with technical expertise in AI and design innovation skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Core domains covered include algorithms, AI applications in design and applied deep learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Through acquiring such competencies in the various domains, graduates can apply AI-driven designs to transform the economy and improve lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the SLS holds a repository of lessons for our students to engage with at their own pace, outside curriculum hours.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Could MOE consider recognising a student's commitment to completing all the self-paced lessons, perhaps under the LEAPS 2.0 framework for secondary school students or in some other way?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are modules that are part of the core curriculum – or part of the school curriculum – which the students can access and help them to pace their own learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Within the SLS, there are also modules that are outside the school curriculum or available in other schools, which the students can access at their own time to learn about things beyond the curriculum.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We encourage the students to do so because we would like our students to develop the habit of initiating their own learning and taking charge of their own learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the various examples I have highlighted just now, for example, at the primary school level, many of the things that we do are for exposure purposes, for the students to learn how to be a smart user.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We do not necessarily use it for assessment at all levels.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But if I may give an example, at a higher level, the module at Temasek Polytechnic which they demonstrated to me, the students used generative AI as part of their coursework.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When they use the generative AI coupled with the interior design course, what they figure out very quickly are two things.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, with AI, they can refine the designs very quickly – using, perhaps, half the time that they used to, using the previous method.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But the second thing that they have also learnt and very importantly, is how to sharpen – as the Member said – the prompt required in order to start the whole process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the prompts are not well-crafted, then, you could be doing things very fast, but not necessarily down the correct path.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is what we mean by age-appropriate lessons.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At a certain level, you can apply AI and sharpen the skills necessary at that level.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Different students at different levels learn to use AI at different levels of competencies and sophistication.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Relating to AI readiness, the Minister mentioned about schools preparing students for AI type of work skills.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I just wanted to understand, what is the bridging with the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI), in terms of getting students ready for the AI-type of work?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The second area would be in terms of ethics.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For those in IHLs, when they enter the workforce, it is not just about being able to do the job, but it is also about how we shape the work that is carried out.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I think there is quite a number of grey areas in terms of AI ethics.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: What would be the type of education pathways that we intend to introduce to IHL students to help them to better prepare for AI-types of job roles in the future?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This goes beyond just about giving credit to or informing people that you have used these tools.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But more importantly, to know the downsides that the program or the AI algorithm – after all, it is an algorithm – may bring and some of the biases that may happen in the course of using that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is something that we are very careful about.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We do not start this at the IHL level.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, in one of my visits to the schools, the teachers encouraged their students to use an AI tool to help them craft an essay.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But it is not about the essay that is most important.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: After they crafted the essay, the teachers wanted the students to: first, know the sources of information that the AI draws upon; then, the teachers encouraged the students to critique the AI product so that they can understand the upside and the downside of the product and also, the potential biases that that algorithm has generated.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, it is through such examples that we allow our students to learn to use AI ethically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: My second part of the comments relates to how we are preparing our students for an AI-enabled world.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, at the broader level, it is making sure that our people are smart users – they know how to use this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is easier done – how to use it, how to use it ethically and how to use it intelligently.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The other part is how to prepare our people to be the coders, the people to work on such algorithms.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For that, our belief is that there are certain fundamentals that are important to equip our students across the board for them to get into careers in this track.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we may not teach AI or we may not teach coding specifically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But behind coding, there are certain foundational skills that are very important.
Because ultimately, in this AI-enabled world where there is an overflow of information, three words come to mind when we encourage our students to use AI.
First, the ability to distil, discern and to discover.
Distil: because the world will be flooded with information.
How to distil the information into what is relevant and useful to us, is the first important step.
Discern: because, having done that, it must come with value.
So, it is important to distil and discern.
But, very importantly, our students and our workers, in time to come, must be able to discover, which means to create new value propositions.
In today and tomorrow's world, none of us will be rewarded by regurgitating old knowledge or what I usually say, "No point answering yesterday's questions with yesterday's answers".
What we need, is to prepare our students to answer tomorrow's questions and challenges with tomorrow's solutions ahead of time.
That is where the discovery comes in and that ties in with the emphasis on self-initiated learning so that you take control of the mastery of the content that we want our students to have.

So, these are important skills for us to prepare our students for the AI-enabled world and we are working closely with MCI on the technical part to build up the repository of courses and knowledge for our students.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, during the debate on the President's Address, I spoke on the age of AI and how Singapore needs to survive in it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am glad that MOE is taking a serious look and making a serious push regarding AI in our education system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have got two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The second question is that there are also Clementi parents worried about media literacy in the age of AI.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are concerned about the issue of misinformation – including deepfakes – and this is an ongoing topic of conversation in all our schools and IHLs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think it is not just about schools and IHLs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Actually, across our whole society, we should be equally concerned about this: how to distinguish truth from fake news, right from wrong.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this is a concerted effort and MOE cannot do this alone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will certainly partner all the stakeholders to make sure that we can share the right information – appropriate information – with our students and also the community, so that we all become more informed in the process without being misinformed by others or being proxies for other people's misinformation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the first supplementary question on inequality of access, it is precisely what we have been trying to do, which is to democratise the access.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are very keenly aware that some families may not have access to some of the materials in the past.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But let me just give two examples of how we have done this and continue to do this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the past, some parents might have more resources and then they go and buy more resource materials for their children to read and worksheets to work on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But today, I encourage everyone to check the SLS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you have children who are in the school-going ages, you will find that within the SLS, there is an entire repository of all kinds of materials.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The best teaching resources are available in the SLS.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And your child does not need to just log on to do the homework that is being assigned by his or her teacher.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: He or she can also log on and do many other things that the teachers did not assign them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Recently, I put up a video to illustrate this because a Secondary 3 student, Kairos, demonstrated to me how he took charge of his own learning during the school holidays by accessing the modules on SLS – these are all free of charge, by the way – to learn at his own pace.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this is one way we democratise the access to all the best materials available across our own system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It helps our people to save time; it also allows everyone to have the access to similar materials.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Another example of how we have done this to democratise the access is that we make sure that even students from poorer family backgrounds do not get left out.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is the vivid example of how we have overcome a potential learning loss among such students during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When schools were closed during COVID-19, we did two things.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And, of course, on top of that, for students who are unable to do such things at home, we even opened up the schools to allow them to continue their learning in schools.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Dr Tan, later in this Sitting, we do have a Motion to talk about Building a Safe and Inclusive Digital Society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Considering the danger of fake news and misinformation and the impact on public safety and security, would the Ministry consider adopting a comprehensive framework across Ministries to educate both parents and students, especially the younger children, on the concept of digital citizenship?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Chan, I hope it is a short answer.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I must say that this is an ongoing challenge not just for MOE or MCI; but it is a whole-of-society challenge.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We cannot have reasoned debate, elections and so forth, if we cannot trust the information that we are accessing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think this requires a whole-of-nation effort and, definitely, MOE and MCI will be working closely with all our stakeholders to develop the framework that the Member suggested.
